source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought
finding: Core critique. The split into intrinsic, extraneous and germane load cannot be cleanly made. Intrinsic load is about the material (an object). Germane load is about learner processes. Load only exists when a learner processes something, so material alone cannot carry load.
numbers: Review built on the 35 most frequently cited ISI papers in the field. Not a formal meta-analysis. Published online Aug 2009, Instr Sci 38:105-134.
quote: Intrinsic load refers to objects (the material itself) and germane load refers to processes (what goes on in learning).
limits: Not a clean test. Argument and examples.
agent_relevance: Do not treat task load, noise load and useful effort as three clean additive numbers in the schema. Define each by an operation we can count, not by a label.

source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought (additivity section)
finding: Additivity is a stated premise (Sweller et al. 1998 p.263: intrinsic and extraneous are additive) but there are signs the total is not a simple sum. If intrinsic and germane load are in different ontological categories, adding them is unprincipled. If they are the same category (cognitive processes), they can interact: understanding the material helps the germane processes.
numbers: No direct additivity experiment is run in this paper. It is an argument plus examples.
quote: An important premise of cognitive load theory is that the different types of cognitive load can be added.
limits: Conceptual, not empirical.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold should not compute a total load budget by summing parts. Treat context size, distractors and reasoning demand as interacting, and test the interaction.

source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought (intrinsic load not fixed)
finding: Intrinsic load is said to depend only on element count and interactivity and to be unchangeable by instruction. De Jong cites counterexamples. Klahr and Robinson (1981): children found a Tower of Hanoi variant (all pegs occupied at the end) much harder than the standard one with the same number of moves. Chi (1992): changing ontological category (force seen as a substance) is hard independent of element count. DeLeeuw and Mayer (2008) changed sentence complexity with content fixed, which moved extraneous more than intrinsic load.
numbers: Counterexamples drawn from other literatures. No new data and no numbers given.
limits: Secondhand summary of the cited studies.
agent_relevance: Task difficulty for the model is not only element count. Content type and representation change difficulty too. Do not assume difficulty is a fixed property that restructuring cannot touch.

source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought (germane load is post hoc)
finding: Germane load is explained after the fact. Sweller et al. (1998) explained higher reported load plus better transfer under high-variability practice as germane. De Croock et al. (1998, distillery troubleshooting) found better transfer with high variability but NO higher rated load, so the explanation failed to hold. Stull and Mayer (2007): learners who built their own graphic organizers did worse than those given author-made ones. Called extraneous post hoc, but it could equally be germane overload.
numbers: Counterexample is one study (de Croock et al. 1998). No sample sizes in de Jong's summary.
quote: If learners perform better, a higher cognitive load must have been composed of germane processes; if they perform poorly, a higher cognitive load must have been extraneous.
limits: Falsifiability argument, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Any scaffold claim of the form: more thinking effort is good if it helps, bad if it does not, cannot be falsified. Our rules must name a check that decides which it was (G3, G2).

source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought (same process, different label)
finding: The same process can count as germane or extraneous depending on the learner's expertise or the goal. Gerjets and Scheiter (2003): a surface-emphasizing group beat a structure-emphasizing group on isomorphic problems, and structure-emphasizing learners spent longer learning. The extra schema work was then judged extraneous for that goal. Scott and Schwartz (2007): navigation maps in hypertext were germane or extraneous depending on use.
numbers: Qualitative re-reading of published studies.
quote: germane processes can be considered to be extraneous depending on the learning goal
limits: Interpretation depends on the goal assumed.
agent_relevance: Whether a reasoning step is useful depends on the goal. The scaffold should state the goal before judging a step as waste.

source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought (measurement)
finding: Self-ratings do not separate the load types. Studies that tried (de Jong 1999 three sliders; Gerjets 2006 task demands, effort, navigation; Corbalan 2008; Cierniak 2009 three single questions; Gerjets 2009b five items) gave inconsistent results. The Paas 9-point item was validated on two studies (Cronbach alpha .90 and .82), which de Jong notes makes it behave like a learner trait, not a task-by-learner effect. About 14 studies found performance differences with no rating differences. A few found rating differences with no performance difference.
numbers: Counts are de Jong's tally of studies up to 2009. Not a quantitative synthesis.
quote: raising doubts whether students can themselves distinguish between different types of load
limits: Pre-2010 literature only.
agent_relevance: Do not use the model's own self-report of how hard something was as a load gauge. Use counted signals (disagreement, check failures, length) instead (G1).

source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought (efficiency and recommendations)
finding: The Paas-Van Merrienboer efficiency formula E = (P - R)/sqrt(2) is used inconsistently. Kalyuga et al. (1998) wrote the formula with an absolute value that should not be there. Low performance with low load gives the same efficiency as high performance with high load. De Jong also says the three design recommendations of CLT (fit prior knowledge, drop non-essential information, stimulate deep processing) existed in instructional design before CLT (Dick and Carey 1990, Gagne 1988, Reigeluth 1983). He proposes going back to two classes: processes that produce knowledge and processes that do not.
numbers: Opinion plus a technical reading of the formula.
limits: Argument, not data.
agent_relevance: A single efficiency score hides which side moved. Report accuracy and cost separately in our own evaluations.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
finding: The theory's own revision. Germane load is no longer a third additive component. It now means the working-memory resources spent on intrinsic load rather than extraneous load. It redistributes resources instead of adding a load of its own. Reason given: if germane load simply replaced extraneous load, total load should not change when extraneous load is cut, but many studies show total load falling.
numbers: Educational Psychology Review 31:261-292. A theory update by the original authors, not an independent test.
quote: Currently, we assume that rather than contributing to the total load, germane cognitive load redistributes working memory resources
limits: Authors judging their own theory.
agent_relevance: Matches our design: one budget, with effort moved from waste to useful work. Do not model useful effort as extra cost on top.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) (element interactivity and evidence base)
finding: Element interactivity now applies to extraneous load too (Sweller 2010), not only intrinsic load. Intrinsic load can only be changed by changing what is learned or the learner's expertise. Most reported instructional effects are due to varying extraneous load. In 1998 seven effects were listed. The authors admit many experiments never measured load directly and counted the predicted learning effect as support for the theory.
numbers: Authors' own account.
limits: Self-report of the field's practice.
agent_relevance: Concedes de Jong's point that confirmation came from learning outcomes, not load measures. Be careful quoting CLT effects as proof of a load mechanism.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) (measurement section)
finding: The authors say the Paas rating gives an overall (intrinsic plus extraneous) measure and cannot split types. A single post-phase rating was always higher than the average of per-task ratings (van Gog 2012; Schmeck 2015). They describe the Leppink 2013/2014 10-item instrument as able to tell intrinsic and extraneous apart, and add that only intrinsic and extraneous are distinguished as basic categories.
numbers: They state more evidence is needed. No instrument statistics are given in the text.
limits: Authors' summary.
agent_relevance: Timing of a measure changes its value. Measure at the same point in the loop every time.

source: Kalyuga (2011) Cognitive load theory: How many types of load does it really need?
finding: Argues that germane load and intrinsic load share one foundation (element interactivity and learner knowledge) and that the three-type additive model can be reduced to two. Only the landing-page abstract was seen (full text paywalled).
numbers: Abstract: three separate and additive types of load. Educ Psychol Rev 23:1-19. No numbers.
limits: Abstract only. Position is cited by Skulmowski and Xu (2022), Jiang and Kalyuga (2020) and Krieglstein et al. (2022).
agent_relevance: Supports a two-part view for our scaffold: waste versus essential demand.

source: Sweller (2010) Element interactivity and intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load
finding: Defines intrinsic load as element interactivity and extends the idea to extraneous load. Only the landing-page abstract was seen (paywalled). The content was confirmed through Sweller et al. (2019), which cites it for the claim that element interactivity also determines extraneous load.
numbers: Abstract-level only. No numbers.
limits: Not opened in full.
agent_relevance: Element interactivity is the single formal lever. It can be counted in a task, so a code-checked scaffold can use it as a size signal.

source: Debue and van de Leemput (2014) What does germane load mean? An empirical contribution to the cognitive load theory
finding: Empirical test of germane load with online news pages in three versions: text, pictures, animations (TPA), text and pictures (TP), text only (TO). Germane load ratings were not tied to task characteristics or performance. They tracked learner motivation and absorption.
numbers: Phase 1 N=92 (TPA 30, TP 32, TO 30). Performance F(2,91)=5.605, means TPA .52, TP .65, TO .50. GL with performance r=.045 (ns). GL with focused immersion r=.362, GL with two other absorption scales r=.289 and .401 (p<.01). EL with GL r=-.470. IL with GL r=-.164 (ns). Phase 2 eye tracking N=36, 12 dropped.
quote: GL could not be related to the task characteristics but to learner motivation.
limits: One intrinsic statistic is printed as F=5.748, p=.128, which is internally inconsistent. Exploratory, news not instruction, small samples, between-subjects. Does not test additivity.
agent_relevance: A useful-effort rating may just be engagement. Do not take enthusiasm or length of reasoning as proof of useful work.

source: Debue and van de Leemput (2014) (interpretation)
finding: The authors read germane load as a motivation measure, in line with Schnotz and Kuerschner. They suggest a non-linear link between intrinsic and germane load and note Kalyuga's argument that the two may be redundant. They did NOT test additivity.
numbers: IL-GL r=-.164, not significant. Non-linear link is tentative, not a tested model.
limits: Speculative reading.
agent_relevance: Warns that load labels may measure something else (motivation). Prefer counted, behaviour-based signals.

source: Klepsch, Schmitz, Seufert (2017) Development and Validation of Two Instruments Measuring Intrinsic, Extraneous, and Germane Cognitive Load
finding: Best case for three separate factors in questionnaire data. In Study 2 a three-correlated-factor model fit best by AIC, a one-factor model fit badly, and a two-factor alternative (ECL versus ICL+GCL, plus an ICL method factor) fit about as well. The germane scale was the weak one.
numbers: Study 1 N=97 (48 informed, 49 naive raters; 24 hypothetical tasks). Study 2: 65-95 per task, 17 tasks, only 65 of 95 finished all. One-factor CFI .612, RMSEA .071, AIC 2185. Three-factor CFI .970, RMSEA .021, AIC 845. Two-factor Model 4 CFI .974, RMSEA .021, AIC 862. Naive GCL scale could not tell low from high GCL tasks (F=0.04, p=.84). Study 2 effects: ICL d=.73, ECL d=.94, GCL d=.35. GCL alpha .67 with 3 items, .85 with 2 items. Informed ratings alpha=.25.
limits: German psychology and computer science students. Hypothetical tasks. Self-report. Small samples.
agent_relevance: Even the supportive study has a weak germane scale and a near tie with a two-factor model. Plan on two clear classes, not three.

source: Klepsch et al. (2017) (follow-up note)
finding: The authors note that the link between germane load and learning is not per se to be expected because the load types interact, and that Leppink et al. (2014) dropped their germane scale because it did not correlate acceptably with learning outcomes.
numbers: Seen in the second half of the page only. Latent correlations were not recovered.
limits: Partial reading of the discussion.
agent_relevance: Germane scales are the least stable part of the measurement literature.

source: Jiang and Kalyuga (2020) Confirmatory Factor Analysis of Cognitive Load Ratings Supports a Two-Factor Model
finding: A confirmatory factor analysis of a 12-item questionnaire supported two factors (intrinsic and extraneous). The four items meant for germane load, once reverse-coded, loaded on intrinsic load.
numbers: N=60 first-year undergraduates learning English as a foreign language listening. Two-factor model chi2=54.069, df=53, p=.433. CFI=.994, TLI=.993, RMSEA=.018, SRMR=.077. All loadings above .30 except one (CL11=.28).
limits: Small N (60), one domain, one questionnaire. The authors flag this. A good two-factor fit does not rule out a three-factor fit. Contested by Klepsch 2017 and by Zavgorodniaia 2020 (as cited in Krieglstein 2022).
agent_relevance: Supports reducing to two classes (waste versus essential demand). Suggests the third class is not measurable.

source: Krieglstein, Beege, Rey, Ginns, Krell, Schneider (2022) A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research
finding: Large pooled test of the questionnaires behind the three-load model. Reliability is good. Construct validity is mixed. Intrinsic and extraneous ratings correlate positively across all four questionnaires, which the authors say tends to contradict additivity and suggests learners cannot separate them. Extraneous and germane usually correlate negatively.
numbers: 53 articles, 67 experiments, N=7413, mean age 20.4. Cronbach alpha: ICL .827, ECL .773, GCL .860. ICL-ECL r+: Leppink 2013 .298 (k=25), Klepsch 2017 .350 (k=16), Leppink 2014 about .5, Eysink 2009 .53. ECL-GCL: Leppink 2013 -.086 (ns), Klepsch -.246, Leppink 2014 -.331. ICL-GCL: Leppink 2013 about zero (ns), Klepsch positive.
quote: the positive correlation between the ICL and ECL thus tends to contradict the theoretically stated additivity hypothesis
limits: Only experimental multimedia learning studies in English. Publication-bias tests significant in a few rows. Eysink items all use easy-or-difficult wording.
agent_relevance: The authors still conclude the data seem to support the three-factor model. Their own ICL-ECL result is a caution against treating the parts as independent and additive.

source: Krieglstein, Beege, Rey, Ginns, Krell, Schneider (2022) A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research (criterion validity)
finding: Correlations with learning outcomes follow theory loosely. Intrinsic and extraneous ratings correlate negatively with retention and transfer. Germane ratings correlate positively but weakly.
numbers: Leppink 2013: ICL-retention r=-.061 (ns, k=20), ECL-retention -.114 (k=22), GCL-retention .188 (k=15), ICL-transfer -.188, ECL-transfer -.120, GCL-transfer .173 (k=12). Klepsch 2017: ICL-retention -.195, ECL-retention -.205, GCL-retention .219, ECL-transfer -.261, GCL-transfer .217.
limits: All effects small (|r| below .27). Correlational. Self-report ratings.
agent_relevance: Even where the load model works, effects are small. Use it as a heuristic, not a predictive law.

source: Krieglstein, Beege, Rey, Ginns, Krell, Schneider (2022) A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research (recommendations)
finding: Authors call for new or better-worded questionnaires and for training learners first on what intrinsic and extraneous load mean. They cite Zu et al. (2021): the ability to tell intrinsic from extraneous load depends on prior knowledge. Single-item scales for germane or intrinsic load are called insufficient by measurement theory.
numbers: Recommendations, not data.
limits: Narrative.
agent_relevance: Novices (and likely weak models) cannot report load types reliably.

source: Skulmowski and Xu (2022) Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load
finding: Reviews five design factors that add task-irrelevant (extraneous) load yet help learning or motivation: interactive media, immersion, disfluency, realism and redundant elements. Proposes a cost-benefit model: each extraneous cost is tied to a germane benefit, and the benefit only shows when the test matches the learning outcome.
numbers: Narrative review, no pooled effect size. Educ Psychol Rev 34:171-196.
limits: No quantitative synthesis.
agent_relevance: Do not strip every extra step from the scaffold. Some friction (such as a forced check) buys accuracy. Judge by the outcome test.

source: Skulmowski and Xu (2022) Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load (history of the model)
finding: Gives the lineage: Sweller (1988) had two parts (intrinsic and extraneous), the 1998 model added germane load as an additive third part, the 2019 model removed germane from the additive total and called it germane processing. Calls for a dyadic model (Kalyuga 2011; Leppink and van den Heuvel 2015) became common. Jiang and Kalyuga (2020) support two factors.
numbers: History compiled from the literature, not new data.
limits: Secondary account.
agent_relevance: The theory moved from two parts, to three, and back to two plus processing in about 30 years, a sign the third part is weak.

source: Adapala (2025) Cognitive Load Limits in Large Language Models: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning (ICE benchmark)
finding: First LLM test of extraneous load with a length-matched control. For a capable model, irrelevant text lowered multi-hop accuracy in a graded way. A long control with padding but no distractors did as well as the clean control. Weak models scored 0 everywhere, so the load test only means something above a baseline competence.
numbers: 200 questions, 10 replications each, 5 models. Gemini-2.0-Flash-001: 0.85 control, 0.82 at 20% distractors, 0.78 at 50%, 0.72 at 80%; slope -0.003 per percent load (95% CI -0.004 to -0.002), p<0.001. Long Control 0.82. Residue condition 0.78 (p=0.12 vs saturation). GPT-4o-0613: 0.65 falling to 0.55 at 80%, slope -0.002, p=0.07, with about 32% of outputs missing a final answer (12% after post-processing). Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B and Mistral-7B: 0% in all conditions.
limits: Preprint by one independent author, v2 Sep 2025. The paper itself says load types may interact non-linearly and measurability is hard. Germane segments are used to define intrinsic load, so the framework collapses to two parts.
agent_relevance: Direct support for our context discipline: keep distractors out of the prompt. Run a length-matched control, and gate any load claim on a solvable baseline.

source: Adapala (2025) (framework and caveats)
finding: The paper states the debates openly: lack of reliable multi-item scales and possible non-additivity of intrinsic, extraneous and germane loads. In practice it uses two counts, needed tokens (germane segments, which define intrinsic load) and unneeded tokens (extraneous). The residue (task-switch) effect correlated with embedding similarity of tasks.
numbers: Residue correlation: Gemini r=0.42, 95% CI [0.21,0.59], p<0.01; GPT-4o r=0.35, CI [0.12,0.54], p<0.05. Hop recall for Gemini 0.90 control, 0.75 at 80% saturation; GPT-4o 0.80 to 0.65.
limits: Single-author preprint, not peer reviewed in the version read.
agent_relevance: An LLM load model that works in practice uses two counts, needed and unneeded tokens. That matches the dual-factor critique.

source: Kaiser, Frigessi, Ramezani-Kebrya, Ricaud (2025) CogniLoad: A Synthetic Natural Language Reasoning Benchmark With Tunable Length, Intrinsic Difficulty, and Distractor Density
finding: Maps CLT onto three independent knobs of logic puzzles: intrinsic difficulty d (interacting entities, attributes and clauses), distractor ratio for extraneous load, and task length N as a proxy for germane load. On 22 reasoning LLMs, task length is the dominant stressor. Distractor effects are U-shaped, not monotone, with the worst accuracy at 25-50% needle-to-hay.
numbers: 13 open-weight LLMs x 100 puzzles per configuration (14,000 per model), plus gemini-2.5, gpt-5, o3 and DeepSeek-R1 on 10 per configuration (1,400). Task length N 20 to 50: DS-Llama-70B 0.89 to 0.66, Qwen3-8B 0.71 to 0.40; gpt-5 1.00 to 0.98, o3 0.99 to 0.98. At N=250 only two models above 50% (gpt-5 and o3, near 0.68). Intrinsic d: gpt-5 0.82 and o3 0.80 even at d=10.
limits: Mapping N onto germane load is an assumption the authors flag as debatable. Pure sequential deductive puzzles only. Exact-match accuracy only. ICLR 2026 version exists (not read).
agent_relevance: Length alone hurts most. The germane knob is really a long dependency chain. Keep reasoning chains short and checkpointed.

source: Kaiser, Frigessi, Ramezani-Kebrya, Ricaud (2025) CogniLoad: A Synthetic Natural Language Reasoning Benchmark With Tunable Length, Intrinsic Difficulty, and Distractor Density (model fit)
finding: A binomial logit model with terms for d, log10 N, rho and rho squared and no interaction terms. The quadratic distractor term improved AIC for 18 models. The model is additive on the logit scale and the authors list interaction among d, N and rho as future work, so this benchmark does not yet test non-additivity of the three loads.
numbers: Capacity points at 50% accuracy per axis (ECL50, NT50, ID50) reported per model. Five models had a non-significant quadratic distractor term (including o3, gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash).
limits: Interactions untested. Authors say CLT is an analogy: LLM load is computational, not biological working memory.
agent_relevance: Test the interaction ourselves: do distractors hurt more at high difficulty and long length? Where load types interact, a sum is the wrong model.

source: Kaiser, Frigessi, Ramezani-Kebrya, Ricaud (2025) CogniLoad: A Synthetic Natural Language Reasoning Benchmark With Tunable Length, Intrinsic Difficulty, and Distractor Density (distractor effect by difficulty)
finding: In the appendix plots the U-shape in distractors becomes more pronounced as intrinsic difficulty d rises. At N=20 many models show a clear U. At N=100 the strongest models are nearly flat (about 0.93 to 0.97). By N=250 most curves are flat. This hints at an interaction between the load knobs.
numbers: Figure descriptions only; the paper gives no formal interaction test.
limits: Figure-level observation, not a fitted interaction.
agent_relevance: Hint that load parts are not additive in LLMs either: the effect of distractors depends on difficulty and length.

source: Gap marker: no LLM paper found that tests three-load additivity directly
finding: In this session two LLM papers operationalize CLT load types (ICE and CogniLoad). Neither fits an interaction model across intrinsic, extraneous and germane load. CogniLoad states that to its knowledge no earlier LLM evaluation separated the three loads.
numbers: Search limits: OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned rate-limit errors and the arXiv API returned empty results, so coverage of 2020-2026 is not exhaustive.
quote: no study has based the evaluation of problem-solving capacities of LLMs in CLT by distinguishing these three load types
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search only.
agent_relevance: Treat LLM load-theory claims as hypotheses. A factorial test of distractors by depth by length would be new data.

source: Park (2010) dissertation on additivity of cognitive load factors (from a web search summary)
finding: A secondary summary says Park tested the additivity hypothesis directly and found that combined effects of load factors are not necessarily additive. Not opened: the repository page failed to load (connection reset).
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Second-hand, from one search snippet. Treat as unverified until the thesis is read.
agent_relevance: Candidate to verify in a later pass.

source: Leppink, Paas, Van der Vleuten, Van Gog, Van Merrienboer (2013) Development of an instrument for measuring different types of cognitive load
finding: Ten-item questionnaire for the three load types. A three-component solution matched intended types in exploratory work, then was confirmed. Full text could not be opened (paywall), so details come from a search summary and from Krieglstein et al. (2022).
numbers: PCA n=56 (PhD statistics lecture); CFA on three lectures with ns of 171, 136 and 148; randomized experiment n=58. Behav Res Methods 45(4):1058-1072.
limits: Second-hand numbers. Per Klepsch 2017, the authors dropped the germane scale in their 2014 follow-up.
agent_relevance: Source of the most-used scale. Its germane scale did not survive the authors' own follow-up.
